Lieutenant Alexander Pearson, flying in an army plane from Williams, Ariz., today crossed the Grand Canyon several times and later flew into the gorge, according to word re- ceived here.  Lieutenant Pearson, who won the transcontinental army air race a year ago and who was lost in the Big Bend country of Texas for several days last February, has been detailed by the war depart ment to study the air currents in and over the canyon and also to locate possible landing fields there. BY Associated Press TO Every Evening


Chicago, July 15.—Points in President Harding's program for governmental assistance in the recovery of commerce and industry, were outlined by Secretary Hoover in an address here today before the National Association of Real Estate Boards.


This great economic program of our President includes, Mr. Hoover said, revision of our tax system, reduction of governmental expenditure, settlement of the tariff, re-organization of the Federal machinery for more efficient service, reorganization of our mercantile marine, refunding of foreign loans, relief of the world from armament, assistance to exporters of our commodities, upbuilding and safeguarding of our foreign commerce, assistance to our farmers by mobilization of private credit, expeditious settlement of the obligations of the government to the rails, announcement to development of our great power resources, the systematic elimination of wastes in production and research and education upon improvements in distribution.


The question of the purpose and place of the government in expediting economic recovery is raised in Washington every hour of the day. Mr. Hoover continued


Unless we would destroy individual initiative and drive ourselves straight into naturalization or internationalism, reduce or raise wages, or deal in commodities, no matter how it is camouflaged.


One of the most difficult problems, the secretary declared, is that of housing. Estimating that nearly 80 per cent of the population are living as tenants, he asserted that nothing is worse than an increased tenancy and landlordism in the country.


There are, he contended, three fields in which the government can be of assistance in remedying the housing situation.


First he said, The government must, as a matter of primary duty, drive every combination out of business that attempts to restrain trade.


Second, the government, to some degree, directly or indirectly, controls or obstructs the flow of credits and is, therefore, has responsibility toward this part of the problem.


Third, the government can and should interest itself in dissemination of information, in scientific study of certain problems in materials and methods and in cooperation with the industries to receive voluntary reduction in wastes, that the costs of homes may be decreased.

The party started at 3 o'clock Sunday morning at Caldwell, making the trip with only one stop at Jordan Valley, where they had breakfast at 9 o'clock.

Trouble was expected along the road, as it was rumored at Caldwell that friends of the two men were expected to make attempts to get them away from the officers along the road. As a precaution against a plot of this sort the two men were heavily chained and close guard was kept over them all the way. Eleven men, besides the ones already mentioned, and including sheriffs, deputies, state constable and the district attorney from Caldwell, and Constable Hoover of Fallon, accompanied the party as far as Jordan Valley, where all the Idaho officers excepting the three above mentioned, turned back.

It is believed by officers that the two men are desperate characters and there is a long string of crimes charged against them. They are accused of stealing an Auburn car at Nampa recently, then robbing a store at Vale, Oregon; later stealing another car at Fallon, robbing business places and shooting Sheriff Smith of that city, and then the theft of the Essex roadster here and the breaking into of the Standard Oil plant. They have been positively identified by Constable Hoover of Fallon as the men who shot Sheriff Smith and have been identified by others as the men who stole the Auburn car, as well as the Essex. Snyder already has a prison record. Tex Smith is a well known rider, having won championships at Pendleton and Calgary, and honors in several other places.

When brought into this city Sunday night the men appeared surly, but when interviewed by a representative of this newspaper yesterday morning they appeared in good spirits and anxious to talk. They stated that they had tried to get hold of a reporter at Caldwell in order to get their own story in the papers, but had been allowed to talk to no one. They said that the Boise papers had printed all kinds of untrue things of them and that they had particularly objected to that on account of that being their home town and the home of so many of their friends. They appeared confident of their being released in the near future, stating they had a good alibi and that as soon as the right time came they would spring it. They said they had a great many friends in Idaho, including an attorney whom they had employed to plead their case; said they could account for where they had been for the past month and that this was the first time they had been in the state of Nevada.

This statement of the question has the merit of originality but the arguments are not sound.

Granted that a teacher unaccustomed to schoolroom visitors may be somewhat timid, and unintentionally imparts some of the nervousness she feels to those in her charge, all the greater reason exists for her and them to wear off that shyness and there is but one way—by practice in working and reciting before outsiders, whose presence affords a natural stimulus to their very best effort. The bond of sympathy between home and school created by frequent parental visits, produces an interest in school work on the part of the child that can come in no other way—his parent and his teacher know each other and are friends, and parents and teachers are inclined to be less critical and fault-finding when difficulties arise, for the same reason—they know each other and are friends. Moreover, there is no place where a teacher can so well remember and discuss each child's particular case as in the school atmosphere. Social gatherings and after church are not the places for discussions of this kind, for even though they may be refreshing to the parent, they should not be imposed upon the teacher at any time.

Frank was one of the leading business men of that town, Jacksonville, Ill.—a 32d degree Mason and a cracking good fellow. The doctor said, "Something tells me I ought to go and speak to Frank."

My friend said, "Go."

He said, "I will pray every minute."


He walked out to that beautiful home and there Frank sat upon the veranda, and Dr. MacFarland said, "I have come up to ask you to be a Christian, Mr. Falkenberg."

New York, April 19.-Flags of every republic of the two Americas waved above the crowds today gathered to witness the unveiling of the bronze figure of Simon Bolivar, South Amer ican liberator, on Bolivar Hill, Gen. tral Park.

 In New York for the first time since his inauguration, President Harding undraped the statue. Mem- bers of the cabinet, justices of the United States supreme court and Latin American diplomats stood with the president on the speakers stand as he paid tribute to the George Wash lngton of South America" Dr. Estaban Gil Borgas, minister of foreign affairs of Venezuela, made the presentation of the statute as gift to the city of New York from his country. Speeches were made by rep resentatives of five nations freed by Bolivar's armies.

 A halfmile long procession of sold iers, sailors and civilians marched be- tween thronged pavements up fifth avenue and across fifty-ninth street to Bolivar Hill.

 This morning, mounted police es- corted the presidents party from the Pennsylvania station to the Waldorf Astoria where they met Dr. Gil Bor- gas, Governor Miller of New York, Mayor Hylan and citizens commit tee. Immediately after the unveiling ceremonies are concluded, the presi- dent will return to Washington.

 This evening the mayors reception committee will give a banquet at the Hotel Baltimore in honor of the Vene- zuelan mission. Later the visiting diplomats will go to the Father Knick- erbocker Ball at the new Hotel Am bassador.

 Copies of a new volume on the life and works of Bolivar were given to President Harding and members of. his party at the foot of the monument. The book, written by Guillermo A. Sherwell, is a complete history of the warrior, statesman, patriot, who crushed the power of Spain in the new world, and yet who died in pen niless obscurity.

visited by thousands and it is desired

Made in Mud.

undiscovered mud that hardened

strata exposed the tracks again to the

Dr. W. D. Matthew, curator of the

lizards.


The climate of the Connecticut Val-

herst college to have been something
like that of Arizona today, hot and
dry, though not tropical. Some of the
dinosaurs are supposed to have been
carnivorous, while other species sub-

Question: I have followed with great interest and appreciation your investment notes. Your columns have been remarkably free from error. You have twice, however, referred to the New Orleans Terminal per cent bonds being guaranteed by the Southern Railroad and by the Frisco. Did not the Frisco guarantee end in this case with the receivership of that road several years ago? To-day I noticed that you render decision in favor of Union Pacific over Canadian Pacific as an investment stock. Does not the Canadian Pacific enjoy the following advantages over its great American rival: 1) lower bonded debt per mile, 2) great working capital and surplus, 3) a longer and better dividend record, 4) greater and more profitable subsidiary interests that would help to bolster the dividend in lean years? Union Pacific has large investments in other railroads, the income from which has been decreasing, while the C. P. without taking into account its great land holdings, has other investments in liquid securities, in government advances, valuable hotels, shipping, etc. Its other income has been increasing. Also the Canadian road has not used proceeds from land sales for dividends, but has kept them in an outside depreciation reserve, it might be termed. Union Pacific's earnings, as you are running at present, roughly double the earnings of the Canadian road, but after allowing for the recapture of earnings by the United States government the two figure up about the same. I believe I am bothering you with this viewpoint because it would appear that the two stocks deserve the same investment rating, on the above figures, and I would be greatly interested if you have knowledge of any other factor that gives the preference to Union. Personally, I should feel safer with the Canadian stock, and hold fifty shares of this to five of Union. I have also bought gold rights, and forty-two shares Pullman, other holdings (bonds, chiefly electric power and telephone.) It is my belief that if these well managed corporations are not to be permitted to keep the earnings that they undeniably can make, there would be few safe investments for a business man, such as myself, other than United States and Canadian government bonds. Being an optimist, where my country and Canada are concerned, I do not look for this, nor believe, does The Tribune expect it. A. L.

Answer—You are right. In 1918 the St. Louis San Francisco defaulted its share of the interest on the New Orleans Terminal per cent bonds. The stock of the company was owned jointly by the Frisco and the Southern; the Southern assumed sole guarantee on the Terminal as it took all of the Terminal Co.'s stock, and the courts have upheld it. The Canadian Pacific is unquestionably one of the strongest railroad companies in the world, and has retained for itself all of the profitable collateral businesses which are more or less intimately connected with a railroad, in contrast to so many roads in the States that relinquished these enterprises to other companies.

Union Pacific, however, is a great banking corporation as well as a well managed, well located and profitable railroad company. There is one danger which the Canadian Pacific faces which does not appear to be confronting the Union Pacific. The entire mileage of Canada may be roughly divided in two parts, one of these belongs to the Canadian Pacific, the other now belongs to the Canadian government. The Canadian government fixes rates for both. As long as the rates are fixed high enough to permit the government railways to earn their operating expenses, and even per cent on the government investment, our opinion is that the Canadian Pacific 10 per cent dividend is perfectly secure. If the government were to cut rates, calling on the taxpayer to make up the deficit, the Canadian Pacific might have a hard time. We don't believe it will happen.

Now the situation has been somewhat reversed. A great point is made of the fact that the President of the United States issued the call for disarmament conference. England is not in the position of having forced the issue though if the truth were told she was eager in private to have America make the move and she has managed to manoeuvre things around so as to go into the conference without any especial responsibility for compelling agreement. Whole Question of Peace

That is not all, however. Tied up with the disarmament problem is something else besides naval expenditures. It touches the whole realm of international peace—the league of nations as an instrument for preservation of peace in the absence of large armaments or some other international body able to accomplish a similar result. Then, too, there are the big financial questions—the payment of war debts—which sooner or later touch the disarmament problem.

America as a disinterested nation and world, with a big navy and with no special interest or ambitions except the peace of the world, is counted upon as a greater moral force in a disarmament conference than ever before. There have been international conferences on armament questions before. The subjects were discussed at The Hague, as well as at the famous London conference of 1908, but no single power had then as much influence as the United States has today. This, of course, is because of the way the United States used her power in the World war—unselfishly and disinterestedly. The success of the disarmament conference called by President Harding doesn't depend upon formulas but upon something entirely different—the readiness of the powers to agree upon a program of peace that will remove sources of friction and possible war. Everybody admits that the chances of war in Europe are remote for physical resources of Europe are too near exhaustion for anyone to rattle the sabre. But there are war clouds in the Pacific. Japan and the United States have delicate issues at stake and so have various British dominions like Australia and Canada and New Zealand. The British Empire and the United States must clear the Pacific of possible trouble before there can be any progress toward disarmament. Accordingly the conference summoned by Mr. Harding is in reality a concrete step toward war prevention—an effort to preserve peace by going at the roots of trouble while they are still, not when the passions of the peoples are influenced by an untoward incident.

Exceeds Borah's Plan.

Senator Borah's resolution has been a contributing factor toward the bringing about of the big conference, but at the same time the President has gone much farther. He has not limited the meeting to Great Britain, Japan and the United States as the Idaho senator wished. He has asked Italy and China to join, the former because she is a member of the supreme council and the latter because much of the trouble in the Pacific relates to the commercial rights of Japan and other foreign governments, including Italy.

In a nutshell the significant statement issued here explaining the relationship between the disarmament conference and discussion of the problems of the Far East is an official admission that Japan must be reckoned with. For many months it has been apparent that Europe and the United States were ready for a program of limiting armaments but the Japanese were hesitant. Naturally they would be when there are so many unsettled questions in the Far East—all the way from the dispute over cable communications at Jap to the Siberian problems and the difficulties over equality of commercial opportunity. The big conference has been called, however. That means much. But like the Irish peace conference it is too early to be overconfident of results. The biggest task is still ahead—a task left unfinished at Versailles and still unaccomplished—namely, bringing the whole world into agreement on a program of preserving peace so as to make armament unnecessary.

Keith was called to the chair, and, on motion, the following report from the Committee on Resolutions was read and adopted:

It becomes our sad duty to chronicle the death of William Randolph Edgar.

He was born at Upton, Iowa, September 18th, 1851, and died at Ironton, Missouri, on September 26, 1921. He was of Scotch descent and Revolutionary ancestry; his father came to Ironton in 1866. His wife survives him.

Mr. Edgar attended the public schools of Ironton; thereafter graduated from the Arcadia College (which institution was founded by the late Rev. Jerome G. Berryman, of which institution Marvin College is the successor), receiving his Bachelor of Arts Degree in 1870; thereafter for two years attended the United States Military Academy at West Point, having been appointed by the late Robert A. Hatcher; he resigned therefrom and entered the law department of Washington University, St. Louis, Mo. from which he graduated with his degree of Bachelor of Laws in 1875.

Upon completing his education, he returned to Ironton and taught in the public schools of Ironton and Arcadia College.

He was admitted to this Bar April 1, 1876, and began the active practice of his chosen profession.

He was married to Sarah P. Whitworth on October 5, 1880, and there was born of this happy union five children, all of whom are living, namely: Maude, William R., James D., Mary O., and Robert Lee Edgar.

In politics he was Democrat, and served his County as Prosecuting Attorney for several years, as Receiver of the U. S. Land Office at Ironton, as member and chairman of the local Democratic Committee and as a member of the State Democratic Committee, as Mayor of Ironton and as Presidential Elector.

He was a member of and Past Master of Star of the West Lodge, No. 1873 A. F. & A. M., and High Priest of Indian Chapter, No. 11, each of Ironton.

Our departed brother was exceedingly well educated; he was well grounded in the great fundamental principles of the law; he was bold, aggressive, and manly antagonist and ever loyal and true to his client and their interests, and these characteristics made him a very successful lawyer.

He was at all times and under all circumstances an ardent, true and loyal citizen, who loved his country and revered her history more dearly than he loved his life.

To the members of his profession he was brother, another self, foe man worthy of our steel, a man, man, loyal friend, a good lawyer.

Resolved, that in the death of William Randolph Edgar, the Bar of this county, Judicial District and State has lost one of its ablest and most successful members;

That we extend to his wife and children our sincere sympathy;

That copy of these Resolutions be spread upon the record of this Court and a copy be given to the IRON COUNTY REGISTER for publication.

Respectfully submitted,

BENJ. MARBURY,
S. M. DEARING.

The Senate Committee on Reconstruction and Production estimated in March of this year, the total construction shortage in the country at between $4,000,000,000 and $4,000,900,900.

During the world war, private construction and construction of every nature not contributing to war purposes was prohibited. After the signing of the armistice high costs prevented the resumption of genuine construction activities. The investing public in this field has not had confidence in the stability of values; they have not been able to determine if and when the cost of construction reached a point warranting their investment. A return of confidence in values in construction will assure more employment than in any other area. Considering all branches of the construction industry, more than 6,600,900 people could be employed if construction would be resumed.

To Secure Confidence.
There are three outstanding factors in the building and construction situation which have the greatest bearing on the resumption of construction activities. They are financing, material costs, and labor costs.

These factors present questions which cannot be settled in a mathematical way; they must be investigated by those interested in each community for itself. The questions are:

1) Can the prospective investor finance the operation at a reasonable cost, reasonable terms and in reasonable volume and free from demands for bonuses and commissions of a questionable character?

2) Does the cost of construction materials to the prospective investor properly represent the reduction which has been made in the wholesale prices?

3) Is labor in the particular locality working at fair rates and giving fair value in the quantity and quality of work done?

If local conditions prove satisfactory, there is no reason why work should not proceed immediately. This is especially true for persons contemplating the building of their homes who are now paying rentals based on inflated values. That this fact is being realized is shown by current statistics. During the month of September of this year, residential building amounted to 80 per cent of the total valuation of contracts awarded in that portion of the country north of the Ohio and east of the Mississippi rivers.

The savings deposits of the people are the natural economic source of loans for home building. The aggregate is ample for this purpose even though a portion is protected by adequate investment in more liquid securities to meet withdrawals. There would be no difficulty in the financing of homes if the fundamental principle of the use of long-term deposits for home loans and long term purposes were generally followed.

In every section of the country owners have declined to start new projects on account of the financing charges, both the interest rate and the commissions and premiums paid for floating loans being discouragingly high. Commissions and premiums varying between 10 and 20 per cent have been charged in addition to from 1 to 5 per cent interest. For example, before the first work of construction was begun the owners of an apartment house were required to pay for the million and a quarter involved an interest rate of 8 per cent, and a bond premium of 1 per cent, and a floating charge of 10 per cent, making total financing charge of 19 per cent. The financing charge of subsequent loan of $250,000 for the same structure was $4,000. This is a charge of 80 per cent. It is doubtful whether the margins received by the architect, the contractor, and by all the producers in the basic industries involved aggregated a sum equivalent to these financing charges.

When an owner must pay such a sum before construction work even starts, many projects have necessarily been abandoned in the face of a continual need and demand for building.

While excessive financing charges for building have not been exceptional, many savings banks, trust companies, and insurance companies have maintained a conservative loaning policy with regard to real estate and home building and the building and loan associations of the United States, with their two and half billion dollars of assets have been conducted with exceptional efficiency. Underlying the whole matter of the financing of construction there is, however, the sound banking principle that long term deposits and the savings accounts of the people should primarily be used for long-term purposes and should not be intermingled with speculative and commercial business.

While trustees of a hospital cannot control
the fees charged by surgeons who use its
operating rooms, the trustees of the
Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore have
issued what amounts to a protest against
extravagant fees. They announce that the
maximum sum that any surgeon ought to
charge, no matter how wealthy the patient
may be, is $1,000.


Even though surgeons are in the habit of
performing many operations for nothing, it
will seem to the average man that the sum
mentioned ought to be adequate. Yet it is
notorious that surgeons have charged from
$1,000 to $5,000 for operations merely be-

St. Augustine, Fla., Feb. 10.—Callers offering advices on many subjects poured in on President-elect Harding here today as soon as he opened his office after three weeks vacation. So long was the waiting line of prominent men and women asking for the president elect's time that he made little progress with his correspondence or with any of the other accumulated business with which his desk is piled high.

If the day's conversation produced any definite development toward solution of the big problems ahead, there was nothing on the surface to indicate it. Despite the influx of visitors, however Mr. Harding slipped away during the afternoon for a game of golf.

Although there was nothing today pointing to decisive developments in regard to the cabinet, the day did not pass without its offering of advice on the subject. Senator Phipps of Colorado brought to Mr. Harding's attention his friend C. C. Dorsey, a Colorado lawyer whose qualifications he urgently set forth for the post of secretary of the interior. Denver, Colo., June 20.—Supporters of Samuel Gompers and John Lewis president of the United Mine Workers, who announced today his candidacy, tonight were marshalling their forces for the contest which will decide whether the veteran labor leader shall be returned to the presidency of the American Federation of Labor.

Both sides are making canvass of the situation and already declare they have mustered sufficient votes to win.

The Gompers forces went into action immediately following the announcement by Lewis, with a declaration that the veteran labor chief would be a candidate and had no intention of withdrawing from the race.

Mr. Gompers, however, said: "If I consider the position of president of the American Federation of Labor so exalted and dignified, I would not stoop to politics to attain it.

No man in this convention, or out of it, can truthfully say, and I do not believe he would untruthfully make such a statement, that I discussed the presidency with him or asked him for his vote."

Except for his brief announcement that he was candidate Mr. Lewis declined to make any statement. His supporters, however were active and claimed that they had pledged more than twenty thousand of the 35,294 votes in the convention.

Although electioneering on behalf of Lewis has been in progress for a week his announcement came as a surprise to many delegates who had believed that he would formally withdraw from the race.

Labor leaders pointed out tonight that the candidacy of Lewis would change the whole political complexion of the convention. They said that there probably would be candidates put into the field in opposition to the present members of the executive council. Up to tonight however, there had been no indication of such a move.

Mr. Lewis has established a campaign headquarters at one of the downtown hotels and is being aided in his campaign by large force of mine worker officials.

Reports that he would not be able to control the votes of his own organization were denied tonight by his supporters, who announced that the four thousand two hundred fifty-seven votes of the miners would be cast in favor of their leader.

The candidacy of Lewis is the first serious opposition that President Gompers has had since 1894 when he was defeated for reelection by John McBride, mine worker. Since that time he has been reelected year after year by a most unanimous vote.

Published reports that representatives of certain anti-Gompers interests are operating among the delegates with a hundred thousand dollar "slush fund" have created considerable excitement. Attempts, however, to get the convention to investigate the matter failed today on a point of order, but it is expected that a motion for a committee of inquiry will be made tomorrow.

ATLANTIC CITY, Sept. 22.—The directors of the National Association of Credit Men gave out statement here to-day criticizing the suggestion that the normal tax on corporate earnings be increased from 10 per cent to 15 per cent, and recommended the following tax program:


"1.—THE excess profits tax should be repealed.


"2.—Income taxation, embodying as it does the principle of taxing in accordance with ability to pay, should be the cornerstone of our Federal system of taxation.


"3.—The income tax should be levied on the income of individuals only, and not on corporations as such.


"4.—Wherever individuals permit their earnings from corporate business to accumulate in the hands of corporation, and thus evade individual income tax, tax comparable to individual income tax should be levied on such earnings in the hands of the corporation.

Drummond looked at the speaker fascinated. He had a sudden feeling that he must be dreaming—that in a moment or two he would wake up and find that they had really been talking about the weather the whole time. Then the cynical gleam of triumph in Peterson's eyes acted on him like a cold douche.

He held open the door for his visitor, and followed him into the passage. At the other end stood Denny, systematically busting a bookshelf, and Peterson glanced at him casually. It was characteristic of the man that no trace of annoyance showed on his face. He might have been an ordinary visitor taking his leave.

And then suddenly from the room outside which Denny was busting there came low moaning and an incoherent babble. A quick frown passed over Drummond's face, and Peterson regarded him thoughtfully.

"An invalid in the house?" he remarked. "How inconvenient for you." He laid his hand for a moment on the soldier's arm. "I sadly fear you're going to make a fool of yourself. And it will be such a pity." He turned toward the stairs. "Don't bother, please; I can find my own way out."


THREE.


Hugh turned back into his own room, and lighting his particularly noisy pipe, sat down in his own special chair. He was under no decisions as to the risks he was running. Underestimating his opponent had never been a fault of his, either in the ring or in France, and he had no intention of beginning now. The man who could abduct an American millionaire, and drug him till he was little better than a baby, and then use a thumbscrew to enforce his wishes, was not likely to prove over-scrupulous in the future.

After a while he began half-unconsciously to talk aloud to himself. "Two!" he remarked, stabbing the air with his pipe. "One—drive the Potts bird up at Berners street; two—do not. Number one is out of court at once. Preposterous! It is absurd. Therefore two holds he held." He rang the bell.

"James," he said, as the door opened. "Take a piece of paper and a pencil—if there's one with a point—and sit down at the table. I'm going to think, and I'd hate to miss out anything."

His servant complied, and for a while silence reigned.

"First," remarked Drummond, "put it down. They know where Potts is. Two—they will try to get Potts."

"Yes, sir," answered Denny, writing it down.

"Three—they will not get Potts. Now, James, you've got to do something else. Rise, and with your well-known stealth approach the window, to see if the watcher still watcheth without."

The servant took a prolonged survey, and finally announced that he "had to see him."

"Then that proves conclusively that he is there," said Hugh. "Write it down, James. Four—'Owing to the watcher without, Potts cannot leave the house without being seen.' Five—'Potts must leave the house without being seen, if we want him.' James, I want him all to myself. He shall go to my cottage on Black River, and you shall look after him."

"Yes, sir," returned James dutifully.

PRESIDENT HARDING'S message, delivered to Congress yesterday, contains no new cures for the political ills of the world and no new theories for the national salvation. It is, however, one immensely notable and reassuring because of its courageous common sense. In the campaign which resulted in his triumphant election, a favorite charge of the opposition was that Mr. Harding was Senate trained; that he would follow not his own views and policies but those of a Senate group with which he was alleged to have been closely allied. Every public utterance and every action of the President up to this time has disapproved that charge and has shown Mr. Harding to be possessed not only of the ability to lay down a broad and wise national policy and follow it, but likewise of the stalwart courage that persists in carrying out public policy to which he is bound, regardless of the wishes of any group, clique or association of influences.

In this message the President is found vigorously urging national action to encourage cooperative marketing, as urged by the agricultural bloc in the Senate; standing outrageously by his demand that revenue revision be made sufficiently complete to take the chains off of business and industry; proposing a constitutional amendment to put an end forever to tax free securities as a refuge for capital seeking to hide from the tax agents of the government; insisting upon prompt enactment of the permanent tariff law to hasten the so greatly needed stabilization of industries; asserting that the public has a right to impose regulations in its own protection equally upon capital organized in corporations and upon labor organized in unions; recognizing the rights of both but protesting special privilege for either.

The President's statement of this nation's obligation to the world in distress and to itself, is one that is very sure to find cordial approval among his fellow citizens. "With all my heart," he said, "I wish restoration to the peoples lighted by the awful world war, but the processes of restoration do not lie in our acceptance of like conditions. Dan T. Hanna. capitalist, merchant,
newspaper proprietor and politician,
died Of complication of diseases early
yesterday morning at hts home at
Croton-on-Hudson. He was a son Of
the late Marcus Alonzo Hanna, United
States Senator from Ohio and one OF
the national leaders of the Republican
party during the Mckinley Admins
trstion. Born at Cleveland, Ohio, ON
December 26, 1856, he grew up to be
his fathers partner and successor in
great coal, iron and shipping busi-
ness at Cleveland and elsewhere. ths
concern being known as NJ. A. Hanna
q Son. He also inherited his fathers
inclination toward politics. In 1912 Mr..
Hanna was one. Of the most enthusiast
tic supporters Of the Progressive move
ment, being one of the active workers
IN the Roosevelt campaign Of that year.
He contributed literally TO it's funds.
and was credited with influencing many
thousands Of Ohio voters to cast Pro-
gressive ballots. Four years later he
returned with the other Progressives
to the Republican ranks, and last year
advocated the nomination Of General
Wood for President


Founded School Of Journalism


In addition to his great industrial
and mercantile establishments at
Cleveland and elsewhere, Mr.. Hanna
became interested in journalism. In
1910 he purchased "The Cleveland
Leader and News" and thereafter de-
voted much attention to it as its pro-
prietor. Three years later he founded
a school of journalism at Western Re-
serve University, with an endowment
of $4,000 year.


Mr.. Hanna's domestic affairs were
frequently exploited in the courts and
in the public press through the divorce
proceedings by which he was sepa-
rated from each of his four wives. He
was first married, before attaining his
majority, in 1887, to Miss May Har-
rington, Of Cleveland, who bore him
three sons, and then in 1898 divorced
him and married Edmund K. Stallo.
His second wife was Mrs. Daisy Cor
don Maud, divorced wife Of Captain
Walter De S. Maud, Of the British
army, who bore him q daughter, and
then in 1907 divorced him and married
Frank D. PeIton.


Final Divorce Last April


Immediately after this divorce Mr..
Hanna married Mrs. Marie Stuart
Skelly, who had been divorced from
Frank E. Skelly, a hotel clerk. She
bore him three children. and in 1915
obtained divorce. A little later in
the same year he married Mrs. Molly
Covington Warden, from whom he was
separated in 1918, and who obtained a
divorce from him in April last.


One Of his sons by his first wife,
Dan r. Hanna jr., of Cleveland, was an
officer in the American Expeditionary
Forces in the late war. His other sur
viving children are Marcus Alonzo
Hanna and Carl H. Hanna, OF Water
town, N Y, and the Misses Elizabeth,
Natalie, Ruth, Charlotte and Mary
Hanna. He also is survived by his
mother, Mrs. Marcus Alonzo Hanna, of
Washington, and two sisters, Mrs.
Medill Mccormick, wife of Senator Nc
Cormick, of Chicago. and Mrs. II. A.
Parsons, Of Cleveland.

Lake Junaluska, N. C., Aug. 12.—Calling upon all true friends of the League of Nations to give President Harding every opportunity to perfect the suggested association of nations, Hamilton Holt of New York, one of the leaders of the pro-league Republicans, speaking here tonight at the Laymen's conference of the Methodist Episcopal church, south, declared that the president soon must choose between the pro-leaguers in his cabinet whom he made and the bitter-enders in the senate who made him.

"Let our political leaders make no mistake," said Mr. Holt. "The league issue will not be settled until it is settled right. Every friend of international peace and progress therefore must withhold final judgment until Mr. Harding sees fit to disclose the detailed plans of his association. But this is clear. If he wants the permanent support of most of the American people his association must be more than a mere group of nations agreeing to be good and peaceable and all revolving about a court.

"The League of Nations. And if Mr. Harding could get the world or the senate to establish a better court with wider jurisdiction than the admirable one just created largely by the genius of Elihu Root and already adopted as the chief tribunal by the present league nations. And if Mr. Harding's association is under no compulsion to do anything except when the spirit moves, the nations would be no better off than they are now with or without an association.

"The present league with its forty-nine members and its truly admirable record of things accomplished in the one short year of its existence is well worth preserving. Indeed, it is better to have the present league continue as it is without the United States during the term of the present administration than to enucleate the league in order to get the United States to enter it. But we cannot wait much longer. The world is on the verge of revolution, famine and pestilence. Mr. Harding must choose between the pro-leaguers in his cabinet whom he made, or the bitter-enders in the senate who made him. The decision must be made reasonably soon. If not, all friends of the league must organize so as to capture congress in 1922 and the presidency in 1924. They must tread the path of the opponents of slavery, who continued fighting even though election after election went against them.

"Nearly all the Democrats and more than half the Republicans—a clear majority of the American people—want the United States to enter some kind of an association with enough teeth in it actually to lessen the probabilities of war. They can win if they unite."

A recent edition of the Dodgeville
Chronicle opposed the construction
of the Mineral Point-Dodgeville road
on the ground that the road was
good enough for the present and
ought not to be constructed until
taxes were reduced.


The Chronicles concern over the
burden of the tax payer is entirely
proper, but it is tardy. 1t did not
manifest itself during the spring and
summer when every other main trav-
elled road leading into the county
seat was being either repaired, relo-
Gated or resurfaced.


Mineral Point has been sadly dis
criminated against in the matter of
decent roads and another year has
gone by with no relief. The Platte
